lead: A beam can twist as well as bend and shear. Torsion is the twisting moment T<sub>u</sub>. It adds shear stresses all around the section, so a beam designed only for bending and shear may crack on the side face. IS 456 avoids a full torsion theory: it converts T<sub>u</sub> into an equivalent shear V<sub>e</sub> and an equivalent moment M<sub>t</sub>. The beam is then designed for V<sub>e</sub> with closed stirrups and for M<sub>t</sub> with longitudinal bars. This chapter shows the conversion, the units and the checks, using a 300 mm × 600 mm beam carrying 30 kN·m.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 for diagonal tension, Chapter 3.2 for stirrup design, and Unit 2 for flexural steel.

blocks.text: Torsion is twisting. A torque Tu, in kN·m, makes shear stresses circulate around a beam section. These stresses are largest near the perimeter and zero at the centre. A thin-walled open section, such as an I-section, twists easily; a closed box or a closed stirrup cage resists the circulation. A solid rectangle is not an open section. Two cases matter. Equilibrium torsion is needed for static equilibrium: a cantilever slab twisting its edge beam, or a curved bridge girder. The full Tu must be designed for. Compatibility torsion comes from restraint: a beam monolithic with a slab cannot twist freely, so the slab attracts torsion. After cracking, the beam loses torsional stiffness and the moment redistributes; many codes allow a reduced design value. Do not mix the two. The diagonal tension background is in Chapter 3.1.

IS 456 does not ask you to solve a full torsion problem. It replaces T<sub>u</sub> by two ordinary actions: an equivalent shear V<sub>e</sub> and an equivalent moment M<sub>t</sub>. The section is then designed as a beam in shear and bending.

blocks.where: V<sub>u</sub> is factored shear (kN); T<sub>u</sub> is torsional moment (kN·m); b is breadth (m); V<sub>e</sub> is equivalent shear (kN). If b is in mm, use V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1600 T<sub>u</sub> / b.
D is overall depth; b and D are in the same units, so D/b is dimensionless; M<sub>t</sub> is in kN·m when T<sub>u</sub> is in kN·m. A deep beam gets a larger M<sub>t</sub>.

items: Convert T<sub>u</sub>, b and D to consistent units.
Check τ<sub>ve</sub> = V<sub>e</sub>/(b d) ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub> from IS 456 Table 20.
Design longitudinal bars for M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub>.

blocks.text: The figure shows this flow for V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN and T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m.

Transverse steel for torsion must be closed stirrups, with ends properly anchored. Ordinary open stirrups do not enclose the concrete and cannot resist the circulating shear. Use the shear route in Chapter 3.2 with Ve in place of Vu. For a two-legged closed stirrup, Asv is the area of both legs; spacing sv follows Vus = 0.87 fy Asv d / sv. Also limit sv to the least of x1, (x1 + y1)/4 and 300 mm, where x1 and y1 are the short and long dimensions of the closed stirrup. Place longitudinal bars for Mt at the corners of the stirrups, at least one bar in each corner, so the torsion steel forms a closed cage. If τve exceeds τc,max, the concrete cannot take the diagonal compression; enlarge the section or increase concrete grade. Do not merely add stirrups. Curtailment and anchorage of these bars follows Chapter 3.5 and Chapter 3.6.

figure.caption: With V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN and T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m on b = 300 mm, T<sub>u</sub> contributes 1.6T<sub>u</sub>/b = 160 kN and V<sub>u</sub> contributes 120 kN, so V<sub>e</sub> = 280 kN. T<sub>u</sub> also gives M<sub>t</sub> = 52.9 kN·m; closed stirrups carry V<sub>e</sub> and longitudinal bars carry M + M<sub>t</sub>.

spec.aria: Shear V_u = 120 kN and torque T_u = 30 kN·m give equivalent shear V_e = 280 kN, where T_u contributes 160 kN and V_u contributes 120 kN; T_u gives equivalent moment M_t = 52.9 kN·m. Closed stirrups carry V_e and longitudinal bars carry M + M_t.

examples.question: A rectangular beam has b = 300 mm, D = 600 mm, effective depth d = 550 mm, factored shear V<sub>u</sub> = 120 kN and factored torsional moment T<sub>u</sub> = 30 kN·m at a section. Find V<sub>e</sub> and M<sub>t</sub>. State what each reinforcement is designed for.
steps: Convert b to metres: b = 0.3 m. The ratio D/b = 600/300 = 2.0.
Equivalent shear: V<sub>e</sub> = 120 + 1.6 × 30 / 0.3 = 120 + 160 = 280 kN. Using b in mm: V<sub>e</sub> = 120 + 1600 × 30 / 300 = 280 kN.

Check equivalent shear stress: τ<sub>ve</sub> = 280 × 10<sup>3</sup> / (300 × 550) = 1.70 N/mm<sup>2</sup>. For M25 concrete, τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 N/mm<sup>2</sup> (IS 456 Table 20). Since 1.70 N/mm<sup>2</sup> is less than 3.1 N/mm<sup>2</sup>, the section is adequate in diagonal compression.
Design closed stirrups for V<sub>e</sub> = 280 kN. Design longitudinal corner bars for M<sub>u</sub> + M<sub>t</sub> = M<sub>u</sub> + 52.9 kN·m.
examples.answer: V<sub>e</sub> = 280 kN and M<sub>t</sub> = 52.9 kN·m, so design stirrups for 280 kN and longitudinal bars for M<sub>u</sub> + 52.9 kN·m.
examples.check:
b = 300.0
D = 600.0
Vu = 120.0
Tu = 30.0
Ve = Vu + 1.6 * 1000.0 * Tu / b
Mt = Tu * (1.0 + D / b) / 1.7
print(round(Ve, 1))
print(round(Mt, 1))

traps: Using T<sub>u</sub> in kN·m with b in mm and forgetting the 1000 factor; or mixing metres and millimetres in D/b.
Treating compatibility torsion as equilibrium torsion and reducing a moment that statics requires.
Designing open stirrups or forgetting corner bars; torsion needs a closed cage.
Skipping τ<sub>ve</sub> ≤ τ<sub>c,max</sub> and adding stirrups to a section that is too small.
Designing longitudinal steel for M<sub>u</sub> alone and forgetting to add M<sub>t</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the IS 456 expressions for V<sub>e</sub> and M<sub>t</sub> in torsion and define every symbol.
quiz.a: V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1.6 T<sub>u</sub>/b, where V<sub>u</sub> = factored shear (kN), T<sub>u</sub> = torsional moment (kN·m), b = breadth in metres for this form, and V<sub>e</sub> = equivalent shear (kN). If b is in mm, use V<sub>e</sub> = V<sub>u</sub> + 1600 T<sub>u</sub>/b. M<sub>t</sub> = T<sub>u</sub>(1 + D/b)/1.7, where D = overall depth (same unit as b) and M<sub>t</sub> = equivalent moment (kN·m).

quiz.q: Why can compatibility torsion be reduced after cracking, while equilibrium torsion cannot?
quiz.a: Compatibility torsion comes from restraint; cracking lowers torsional stiffness and the moment redistributes. Equilibrium torsion is required by statics, so the full value must be carried.

quiz.q: A beam has b = 250 mm, D = 500 mm, V<sub>u</sub> = 80 kN and T<sub>u</sub> = 20 kN·m. Find V<sub>e</sub> and M<sub>t</sub>.
For M25 concrete, τ<sub>c,max</sub> = 3.1 MPa. A trial section gives τ<sub>ve</sub> = 3.4 MPa. What is wrong and what will you do?
quiz.a: The equivalent shear stress exceeds the concrete maximum, so the section is too small for diagonal compression. Increase b or D, or use a higher concrete grade; adding stirrups alone is not enough.

quiz.q: Why are closed stirrups and corner bars required in torsion?
quiz.a: Torsion produces circulating shear around the perimeter. Closed stirrups enclose the concrete and anchor the shear path; corner bars tie the cage and carry longitudinal torsion steel.

quiz.q: In the worked example, if M<sub>u</sub> = 90 kN·m, what factored moment should the longitudinal bars resist?
A beam supporting a cantilever slab develops T<sub>u</sub> = 40 kN·m. Can you use half of it because the slab will crack? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The torque is equilibrium torsion needed for the cantilever's stability. Cracking does not remove the statical requirement; design for the full 40 kN·m.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice, edge beams, curved bridges and spandrel beams are checked for torsion using 3D frame analysis, and the reinforcement is detailed as a closed cage. Research uses space truss and softened truss models, where concrete diagonals and steel ties carry the torque; Eurocode 2 expresses torsion through an equivalent thin-walled tube with a strut angle θ. For a next search, use the terms 'space truss model torsion', 'IS 456 clause 41 torsion', and 'torsion in edge beam'.
